questions.stem: The Dominated Convergence Theorem allows you to conclude $\lim_{n\to\infty}\int f_n = \int f$ provided:

options.text: $f_n \to f$ pointwise and $|f_n| \le g$ for some integrable $g$.
options.explanation: The dominating function $g$ controls the size of all $f_n$. This is the standard DCT hypothesis. No further uniformity conditions are needed.
Uniform convergence is sufficient but not necessary. The DCT is more general — it allows pointwise convergence provided the domination condition holds.
Continuity is not required by the DCT. The theorem applies to any measurable functions satisfying the domination condition.

options.text: The integral $\int f_n$ is finite for all $n$.
options.explanation: Finiteness of individual integrals is a consequence of the domination condition (since $|f_n| \le g$ and $g$ is integrable), not an additional hypothesis.

questions.stem: The Lebesgue measure of the set of rational numbers $\mathbb{Q} \subset \mathbb{R}$ is:

options.explanation: $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable: $\mathbb{Q} = \{q_1, q_2, \ldots\}$. Each singleton $\{q_n\}$ has measure zero. Countable additivity gives $\lambda(\mathbb{Q}) = \sum \lambda(\{q_n\}) = 0$.
Rationals are countable and dense but measure zero. Measure is not the same as density.
The rationals are unbounded, but each point has zero measure. Measure zero times infinity is still zero here (countable additivity applies).

options.text: Undefined — rationals are not Lebesgue measurable.
options.explanation: The rationals are a countable set and therefore Borel measurable. All Borel sets are Lebesgue measurable.

questions.stem: Fubini's theorem guarantees that for an integrable function $f(x,y)$:

options.text: The iterated integrals $\int\int f\, dx\, dy$ and $\int\int f\, dy\, dx$ are equal.
options.explanation: Fubini's theorem allows free interchange of the order of integration, provided $f$ is integrable (or non-negative, for the Tonelli version).
The integral of a positive function is positive. Fubini says nothing about the value, only about the order of integration.

options.text: $f$ must be continuous for the iterated integrals to make sense.
options.explanation: Fubini's theorem applies to measurable (Lebesgue-integrable) functions, which need not be continuous.

options.text: The partial integrals $\int f(x,y)\, dx$ are continuous in $y$.
options.explanation: Measurable but possibly discontinuous functions may have partial integrals that are merely measurable, not continuous.
